clue.text: A hit in the financial district, or a disaster

indicators.note: the first words are placed inside the district named after them

parts.note: the City is London's financial district
taken as written
to lam is to thrash or hit

explanation.surface: A blow struck in the Square Mile, or perhaps a market crash.
explanation.walkthrough: The City of London is the financial district; A and LAM sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A calamity is a serious misfortune or catastrophe, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Four notes tendered by diner

wordplay.note: four musical notes of the scale, C, A, F and E

explanation.surface: A diner hands over four banknotes to pay the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like money being tendered, but it means musical notes, which are named by the letters A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: A diner in the American sense is a small cheap eating place, much like a cafe.

clue.text: Behold the old city glare

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
Ur is the ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A command to look at the harsh glare over an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur is the crossword's favourite old city, the Sumerian city of Abraham.
explanation.definitionFit: To lour (or lower) is to scowl or frown darkly, a close relative of glaring at someone.

clue.text: Space traveller with a stomach upset will undergo change

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: ET is the extra-terrestrial of the Spielberg film
taken as written
tum is an informal word for the stomach

explanation.surface: An astronaut with an upset stomach is about to undergo an unpleasant change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' seems to describe the stomach, but it tells you to turn the whole string upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: To mutate is to alter in form or nature, as genes and organisms do.

clue.text: Indulging a collector's hobby with Spooner's Iberian running

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so the phrase must be treated that way

parts.note: an Iberian country's trotting; swap the first sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone indulges a collecting hobby while running around Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Spain's trotting becomes trains potting once the opening sounds trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainspotting is the British hobby of logging the numbers of locomotives seen, a collector's pastime.

clue.text: Take a double role in part of play

parts.note: to take a role is to act
double suggests two

explanation.surface: An actor takes on two characters in one segment of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all theatre, which suits the answer, a stage division.
explanation.definitionFit: Act Two is the second main division of a stage drama, hence a part of the play.

clue.text: A piece McShane's arranged

indicators.note: things arranged are put in a new order, so the letters of the name get reordered

parts.note: the name with its possessive s, all eight letters used

explanation.surface: An actor called McShane has set up a piece on the board.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s belongs to the fodder, giving eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A chessman is any of the pieces or pawns used in the board game of chess.

clue.text: Sad song writer has detailed trio to incline the head one way

indicators.note: detailed is read as de-tailed, with the final letter cut off

parts.note: a trio is three
to nod is to bow or incline the head
Roman numeral one
St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A melancholy songwriter, playing in a three-piece group, nods along to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'elaborate', but it means losing a tail. ST for street is a standard abbreviation for a way.
explanation.definitionFit: A threnody is a lament or dirge, so whoever composes such mournful pieces is its writer.

clue.text: Which adventure book character wore the monocle?

definitions.text: Which adventure book character wore the monocle?

parts.words: Which adventure book character wore the monocle?
parts.note: surface reading: a quiz question about a dashing hero sporting an eyeglass
setter's reading: a single eyeglass would suit a person who sees with just one eye, a character type in adventure yarns such as pirates

explanation.walkthrough: The monocle points at sight in a single eye; the proverb 'in the kingdom of the blind' supplies the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with only one working eye would need just a single lens, so the monocle is a fitting accessory.

clue.text: Constantly varying complaint by badly cut worker

parts.note: flu is an illness, a complaint

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters of the word next to it come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
the worker ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: An employee who has been cut badly keeps changing the grievance he lodges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance but here means an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluctuant means wavering or unstable, rising and falling irregularly, like prices that never settle.

clue.text: A month is often attributed to this Shakespearean

indicators.note: the play's authorship is shared out among writers, and the letters are likewise dealt out afresh

parts.note: all thirteen letters of these four words are used

explanation.surface: A trivia note says a month is commonly linked to a certain Shakespeare work.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, this play is often attributed partly to Thomas Middleton as co-author, which the surface hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon of Athens is one of Shakespeare's tragedies, about a generous Athenian who turns misanthrope.

clue.text: For high-rise accommodation look around the Royal Institution

indicators.note: around says the first word's letters go on both sides of the institution's abbreviation

parts.note: to eye is to look at
RI is the abbreviation for the Royal Institution

explanation.surface: Someone flat-hunting in a tower block is told to check near a scientific institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-rise accommodation' suggests a tower block; it is a bird's lofty home.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is an eagle's or other raptor's nest, built on a cliff or treetop, so lofty housing.

clue.text: Rough notes on army's type of manual labour

indicators.note: a rough version is crude and disordered, so the letters that follow are taken out of order

parts.note: all twelve letters of the three words are used

explanation.surface: Crude memos about the sort of physical work soldiers do.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive s of army's is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonemasonry is the craft of cutting and laying stone by hand, heavy physical work.

clue.text: The breadth of a footballer at the feast!

parts.note: a wing is a player on the flank of the team
a spread is a lavish meal laid out

explanation.surface: Ridicule of a soccer player's waistline after a big banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is a player getting wider at a feast; the breadth is really that of a bird or plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Wingspread, like wingspan, is the distance from tip to tip of outstretched wings, a measure of breadth.

clue.text: Advance payment, a measure hobo circumvented before the war

parts.note: the ante is a stake paid in before cards are dealt

indicators.note: to circumvent is literally to go around, so the vagrant's word surrounds the measure

parts.note: bum is American slang for a tramp
an ell is an old measure of cloth length

explanation.surface: A tramp is paid up front and dodges an instrument before hostilities begin.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobo and bum are both American words for a tramp; the ante is a poker stake, paid before the deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Antebellum is Latin for prior to conflict, used especially of the American South before 1861.

clue.text: Hostelries popular with Poles

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
the north and south poles, N and S

explanation.surface: Pubs that are well liked by Polish customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people, but it means the two magnetic poles.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are public houses offering drink and lodging, which is what a hostelry is.

clue.text: Liberal with nothing to hide?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: with the palm displayed, concealing nothing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' tempts as politics; it means generous here.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous giver shows an unclenched palm, and a palm spread wide plainly conceals nothing.

clue.text: Three quarters against taking Common Entrance settle comfortably

parts.note: three of the four compass quarters, east, north and south
con means against, as in pros and cons
CE is the Common Entrance exam for British private schools

explanation.surface: Pupils at three-quarters of a school, opposed to sitting an entrance exam, settle in happily.
explanation.walkthrough: Common Entrance is the exam British children sit at about 13 to enter private secondary schools.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensconce oneself is to establish oneself in a snug, safe or comfortable place.

clue.text: Does an environmentalist gorge on cabbages?

parts.note: a Green is an environmental campaigner
to stuff oneself is to gorge

explanation.surface: A question about whether eco-campaigners pig out on cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: The question format reads naturally while the wordplay simply joins the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Green stuff is an informal term for leafy vegetables such as cabbages and greens.

clue.text: One's back among the motorists from the Continent

indicators.note: back says the short phrase before it is read from end to start
among places those letters within the motoring organisation's initials

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, the British motoring organisation
one is I, and 's is is

explanation.surface: Someone has returned to a crowd of drivers coming from mainland Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Continent' suggests Europe to a British reader, but it is the largest continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the largest of the world's continents, stretching from the Urals to the Pacific.

clue.text: Short man, the doctor: about to become an old eccentric, perhaps

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the words before it are taken backwards

parts.note: Reg is a shortened form of the name Reginald
doc is a familiar term for a doctor

explanation.surface: A little GP is on the way to turning into a strange old fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short man' looks like a man of little height; it is a man's name cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: A codger is an informal term for an elderly man, often one with odd or quirky ways.

clue.text: Trippers' coin can be changed according to written direction

indicators.note: if the letters can be changed they may be shifted into a new arrangement

parts.note: all twelve letters of the two words are used

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers' cash can be exchanged as instructed in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Changing money sounds like a bureau de change; here change means rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A prescription is a doctor's written instruction for medicine, so it is a written order or direction.

clue.text: You find this smoother coming up? Me neither!

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: me neither is the same as nor I

explanation.surface: A conversational exchange about not finding something to smooth with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me neither!' reads as a reply in a chat; it is equivalent to the two words nor I.
explanation.definitionFit: An iron is the household appliance that smooths creases from clothes.

clue.text: Live to claim your little cowshed

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so the short verb holds the abbreviation

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
yr is a short form of your

explanation.surface: An invitation to dwell in your own tiny shed for cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' tells you to use the abbreviation of your, not a word meaning small.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a farm building where cattle are housed, a word still used in Scotland and the north.

clue.text: Terry's predecessor, the Spanish student, is taking the French in

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
L for learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
en is French for in

explanation.surface: An earlier Terry, a Spanish student, is studying French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Predecessor' suggests someone earlier in a job; the actress Ellen Terry's first name comes before her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen Terry was the great Victorian actress, so in her full name Ellen stands immediately ahead of Terry.

clue.text: Valley with stream and fish on line — cap that!

parts.note: a glen is a narrow Scottish valley, typically with a stream
the gar is a long-snouted fish
RY is short for railway, a line

explanation.surface: An angler boasts of a valley, a stream and a fish on the line, challenging others to beat it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap that!' reads as 'beat that', but cap is the definition. RY for railway is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A glengarry is a brimless Scottish woollen hat with ribbons at the back, so a type of headwear.

clue.text: In old Amsterdam, self-contained old-fashioned girl

indicators.note: contained says the letters are held within the run of words before it

parts.note: the end of the city and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A self-sufficient, traditional young woman living in historic Amsterdam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-contained' reads as independent; split it, and contained signals the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Damsel is an archaic or literary word for a young unmarried woman, a maiden.

clue.text: Grantees required to be set apart

indicators.note: re-quired suggests something reassembled anew, so the letters are put together again in another order

parts.note: all eight letters of the word are used

explanation.surface: People given grants must be kept separate from others.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange is to alienate or drive people apart so they are no longer close.
